alt: Section A is a compulsory 25-mark question, half of Paper 4. You read 400 to 500 words of unseen text, focus on the specified aspect, select and rank the most important issues, and write an essay linking text details to wider study. It assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4.
caption: Stay on the specified aspect, and rank the issues rather than summarising the text.

after: ## Area 1: the historical development of English as a "global" language
alt: First wave: migration and colonial settlement created first-language communities in North America, Australia and New Zealand, while colonial administration made English a language of government, law and education in parts of Africa and Asia. Second wave: US influence, then global media, science, business and the internet. A note gives Crystal's argument that power, not the language itself, makes a language global.
caption: English spread through power, first colonial and then economic and cultural.

after: ## Area 1: the historical development of English as a "global" language
alt: Five rising steps for postcolonial Englishes: foundation; exonormative stabilisation, with norms imported from outside; nativisation, as local features develop; endonormative stabilisation, when local norms are accepted as standard; and differentiation, as internal varieties emerge.
caption: Postcolonial Englishes move from imported norms to local standards.

after: ## Area 1: the historical development of English as a "global" language
alt: Three views: English stays the main international lingua franca; as more people use English as an additional language, monolingual speakers may lose their advantage and other languages may grow, a view associated with David Graddol; or English fragments as Latin did, which critics think global media makes less likely.
caption: Forecasts diverge: continued dominance, shifting advantage or fragmentation.

alt: Speakers of different languages form a pidgin, a reduced contact language with no native speakers; when children speak it as a first language it creolises into a full language, as Tok Pisin has. Below, the sociolect continuum runs from basilect through mesolects to acrolect, and speakers move along it by setting, audience and purpose.
caption: A pidgin becomes a creole when children grow up speaking it; speakers then shift along the continuum.

alt: Four ethical issues in the spread of English: language shift and death, cultural imperialism (Phillipson's argument, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's choice of Gikuyu and the critics' reply), equality of opportunity, where English can open or close doors, and global cooperation, such as English as the language of international aviation.
caption: The spread of English is neither wholly positive nor wholly negative.

caption: Each paragraph: quote, explain, connect, evaluate; then end with a judgement.
